UK BUYER EDUCATION

Parrot documentation, CITES and UK registration

There is no single paperwork rule for every parrot. The scientific name, lawful origin, proposed transaction, housing arrangements and journey all matter. Use this guide to prepare questions, not to certify an individual bird.

CITES and parrot paperwork: start with the actual bird

There is no single document set that applies to every parrot in the UK. Requirements can turn on the exact species and scientific name, where the specimen originated, whether the use is commercial, the bird’s identification, and whether it will stay in one jurisdiction or cross a border. This guide is a practical prompt for checking those facts, not a legal determination that any individual bird may be sold, kept or moved.

For a proposed transaction, identify the actual bird and the proposed activity before relying on a seller’s summary. Ask for copies of relevant records, compare identity details and dates, and establish who is responsible for any required original certificate or permit. If anything is uncertain, contact the Animal and Plant Health Agency (APHA), the relevant UK administration or the destination authority before payment, contract or transport arrangements.

When might an Article 10 certificate be needed?

Under the current GOV.UK guidance, commercial use of an Annex A specimen normally requires an Article 10 certificate, unless a specific exemption or other applicable route has been confirmed. “Commercial use” is broader than an ordinary sale and the details matter. Do not assume that a bird’s captive-bred status, an old certificate or a seller’s assurance automatically resolves the requirement. Ask APHA which document applies to the particular specimen and proposed use.

Article 60 certificates are for specific qualified scientific institutions and circumstances; they are not the normal retail route for buying a pet parrot. Exemptions are limited and must be checked with APHA rather than inferred from a bird’s history or intended home. The official guidance explains certificates for commercial use and should be consulted directly: GOV.UK: Endangered species certificates for commercial use (updated 23 June 2026).

Annex B specimens do not generally require an Article 10 certificate for domestic commercial use, but the relevant person must be able to demonstrate lawful origin. Ask what evidence supports the bird’s origin and retain clear copies of records. The absence of an Article 10 certificate is not, by itself, proof that a specimen was lawfully sourced or that every other rule is satisfied.

Read the certificate type, holder and limits

A specimen-specific certificate (SSC) travels with the bird for its lifetime and should be transferred with it when the bird changes hands. Check that the certificate’s description and identification details match the individual. Preserve the original as instructed and keep a secure copy for your records. A mismatch, missing document or uncertainty about a condition is a reason to pause and ask APHA, not to guess.

A transaction-specific certificate (TSC) is restricted to the named holder and the activity described. It is not a general pass that automatically follows the bird to a new owner or future commercial use. Before any later sale or other commercial activity, verify with APHA whether a new certificate is required. Confirm the effect of the certificate’s conditions for the exact transaction.

Geography matters too. A GB SSC is valid for Great Britain; a Northern Ireland SSC is valid in Northern Ireland and the EU. They are not universally interchangeable. Do not assume that a certificate valid in one place authorises an activity in another. Check the certificate type, named holder, stated activity, jurisdiction and bird identity together.

Species identification, rings and microchips

Use the common name and scientific name to establish which species is involved; closely related or commonly abbreviated names can cause confusion. The Species+ database can help with species and scientific-name lookups. It is not a certificate-verification service and cannot confirm that an individual bird’s sale or documents are valid.

Where a bird’s certificate refers to a closed ring, microchip or another identifier, compare the record to the actual bird and ask how the identifier was checked. Keep identification information private: avoid publishing full numbers or unredacted certificates. Closed rings and microchips are relevant where applicable, not universal identifiers required for every parrot. Identification alone does not establish lawful origin, ownership or permission for commercial use.

Ask for the date and identity details to be consistent across the certificate, transfer record and any available health or origin documents. If a ring cannot be read, an identifier differs, or the bird cannot be confidently matched to the paperwork, do not treat the discrepancy as a minor clerical detail. Seek guidance from APHA or the issuing authority.

Border permits are different from domestic certificates

An Article 10 certificate or other domestic CITES document is not the same as a permit to import or export a specimen. A border movement can involve CITES permits as well as separate animal-health, customs and route requirements. Confirm the rules for the exact species, origin, destination, purpose and route with the competent authorities before entering into a contract, paying on the assumption a journey can happen or booking transport.

GOV.UK’s CITES imports and exports guidance explains the permit system. Read it alongside the relevant animal-health import or export guidance; a CITES document does not replace those checks. Do not assume a domestic sale document allows a border crossing, or that an animal-health route alone resolves CITES obligations.

Movements between Great Britain and Northern Ireland require particular care. DAERA currently advises that there is no Approved Northern Ireland quarantine facility and direct commercial movements of captive birds from GB are not a routine parcel service. This is not a statement that every GB-to-NI movement is prohibited: purchase and ownership transfer must be distinguished from non-commercial travel with an existing pet, and the proposed route must be checked with DAERA before anyone promises it. See DAERA: Other animal species movements from Great Britain to Northern Ireland.

Bird-keeper registration depends on where and how birds are kept

Keeper registration rules are separate from CITES paperwork and vary across the UK. Do not infer a universal rule from a general statement about “parrots” or “pet birds”. The species, number of birds, housing and activity may affect the answer. Check current official guidance for the home address and the exact setup.

In England and Wales, you must register within one month of keeping poultry or other captive birds, unless an exemption applies; separate official guidance covers keepers of 50 or more. The exemption for psittaciformes (including parrots) and passeriformes applies only when birds are both fully housed in a dwelling or other indoor structure and have no access to the open air. Taking a bird outdoors for exercise or training means you must register. A veterinary visit does not itself remove the exemption, but a bird gathering may require registration: check the event organiser’s licence. Check the GOV.UK bird-keeper registration collection and the guidance for fewer than 50 poultry or other captive birds, updated 30 September 2026. Keep required records and check them at least every 12 months. Notify the authority within 30 days if contact details, species or purpose change, or when you begin keeping 50 or more; if you remain below 50, a change in the number of birds alone does not need updating.

Scotland has a different exemption: under Scottish Government guidance, psittacines are exempt when kept fully indoors with no outside access, or outdoors in a fully enclosed structure. Exercise or training outside that enclosure requires registration. In contrast to England and Wales, the guidance says a veterinary visit or bird gathering does not currently trigger registration by itself. Scotland also has a separate Scottish Kept Bird Register, so check whether it applies.

For Northern Ireland, consult DAERA’s current bird-keeper and movement guidance, rather than applying England, Wales or Scotland rules. Requirements and available routes may change. When in doubt, contact the competent administration before acquiring or moving a bird.

A practical document check before proceeding

  1. Write down the bird’s common and scientific species name, origin, intended use and current location.
  2. Ask what CITES certificate or lawful-origin evidence applies, and whether it is an SSC, TSC or another document. Ask who holds the original and what must accompany the bird.
  3. Compare the document’s holder, permitted activity, validity or conditions, jurisdiction and identification details with the real proposed transaction.
  4. Ask which identification is present, where applicable, and how it matches the certificate. Keep copies securely and protect personal details.
  5. Check separately whether keeper registration, movement permissions or animal-health requirements apply at the destination.
  6. For a border route, confirm permits and the correct animal-health process with the authorities before payment, contract or travel arrangements.
  7. Record who confirmed each point, when, and any conditions still outstanding. Do not proceed while a material identity or permission question remains unresolved.

These questions help organise a conversation; they do not certify a bird’s legality. Ask APHA or the relevant authority to confirm an individual certificate or proposed use. A database species lookup is not individual document verification.
